title: MB2-00572
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The male claimant, XXXX XXXX, and the female claimant, XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Croatia. They are claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 961 and subsection 97(1)2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

Since his childhood, the male claimant has had a life of problems because of his gypsy origins. His children were dismissed by their teacher because they are gypsies. Around XXXX XXXX, 2007, when some individuals were threatening his brother, the male claimant was attacked and injured in the mouth by individuals because he wanted to call the police.
Following this attack, the male claimant was hospitalized and wanted to file a complaint with the police, but they refused to accept the complaint.
After his hospitalization, the male claimant received a hospital bill of 28,000 kunas; however, as he was unable to pay it, he was imprisoned for a period of four months.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, some individuals tried to rape his spouse.

Around XXXX XXXX, 2011, the male claimant was beaten by Croats who told him that he did not have the right to buy bread. The male claimant tried to file a complaint, but the police did nothing. Around XXXX XXXX, 2011, the male claimant was struck by some individuals who threatened to set fire to his wife and children.
Before coming to Canada, some Croats told the male claimant that Hitler should have killed all the gypsies.
He also alleged that his wife was abused and threatened by some individuals who had set upon her while she was gathering empty bottles to sell in order to feed his children.
Essentially, these are the facts alleged by the male claimant in support of their refugee protection claim. ANALYSIS Identity

The panel is satisfied as to the identity of the claimants, which they established by means of documentary evidence on the record, namely certified true copies of their passports, the originals of which were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC).3 Credibility

In his reply to question 31 of his Personal Information Form (PIF),4 the male claimant states that he was injured by some individuals around XXXX XXXX, 2007, when he tried to help his brother. When asked by his counsel where he was coming from when he saw his brother being attacked, the male claimant replied, [translation] "From XXXX," adding that he had gathered scrap metal in XXXX and that he was returning to his home.

When asked to explain why the medical certificate,5 which he filed in support of his refugee protection claim, indicates that he was intoxicated whereas he stated that he was returning from work, the male claimant replied [translation] "Yes, I only wanted to help my brother. They were about 15 individuals." When questioned again on this point, the male claimant stated, "Yes, three or four beers and a tenth of a litre of brandy, nothing much." The panel rejects the male claimant's explanations, which it considers not credible because they do not satisfactorily explain the fact that he was drunk upon his return from work. Furthermore, the panel considers that the male claimant was not telling the truth regarding the events he stated he experienced.

Moreover, according to this medical certificate, the date of hospitalization was from XXXX XXXX to XXXX, 2007, whereas the male claimant stated he was beaten and hospitalized in [translation] "mid-XXXX 2007." Also, according to this same certificate, the male claimant was drunk to the point that he could not describe how he had been injured.

Also, when confronted with the hospital bill6 indicating that, on XXXX XXXX, 2007, he had to pay the sum of 2,254.09, whereas he mentions in his reply to question 31 of his PIF that [translation] "the hospital saddled me with a bill that totalled 28,000 kunas," the male claimant, hesitant and visibly uncomfortable, stated that the bill indicating that he had to pay the hospital the sum of 28,000 kunas was burned in Croatia.

The panel rejects the male claimant's explanation, which it finds not credible because it was obvious that he was improvising a reply to try to justify the noted contradiction. This leads the panel to doubt that the male claimant was imprisoned for non-payment of the bill. Also, the panel considers that the male claimant did not state the truth regarding his injuries and his hospitalization.

Furthermore, concerning this hospital bill and the medical certificate, it is important to note that these two documents are at the heart of the male claimant's refugee protection claim, because he stated that in mid-XXXX 2007, because of his gypsy origins, he was beaten and hospitalized.

Moreover, when confronted with his reply to question 41 of his refugee protection claim form,7 which indicates "I have not experienced persecution in my life," the male claimant stated [translation] "I never was. But, I had to flee because I could no longer take the abuse. The children came from school; they had pulled their hair. Now, life is respected. Unfortunately, if the children are taken out of school. I may be illiterate, but at school we are rejected because of our nationality. I decided to really leave. I am prepared to be imprisoned in Canada as I am not badly treated. If I must return there, at 13 or 14 years old, they no longer have the right to go to school. I do not want them to be illiterate like me because they can no longer go to school. I have experienced many things in my life, but I do not want my children to experience the same things, and this is why I asked for help from Canada."

Although the male claimant's wishes regarding the future life of his children are most commendable, the panel is unfortunately not here to hear the case of his children, as they are not part of this case.

Having said that, regarding the male claimant's explanations about his statement in his refugee protection claim form, namely, that he was not persecuted in his country, the panel can only find that his explanations do not satisfactorily justify the contradiction noted, especially as in question 42 of this same form, he indicates that he did not fear anybody in his country.

Furthermore, in question 43 of his refugee protection claim form, he states that he came to Canada so that he and his family could have good living conditions. The panel understands that collecting scrap metal and bottles in containers in order to sell them to be able to feed his family does not constitute very easy economic conditions. However, the panel has no jurisdiction with respect to humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

Moreover, at the hearing, the male claimant stated that what had prompted him to leave Croatia had occurred only in 2012. He was forced to go to the police station because he was suspected of stealing a bicycle. Once at the police station, he was threatened and beaten. He added that this happened two or three months before arriving in Canada, namely, in XXXX or XXXX 2011.

When asked why this important fact was not in his reply to question 31 of his PIF, the male claimant replied, [translation] "I thought that there was sufficient evidence, and I was still in shock." Hesitantly, he added, "I am not lying."

The panel rejects the male claimant's explanations, which it considers not credible because it finds it implausible that the male claimant did not mention in his reply to question 31 of his PIF a fact as important as this event, because this time he stated that he was beaten by the police and following this incident, he decided to leave Croatia. Therefore, this event is the trigger that prompted the male claimant to leave Croatia.

Furthermore, regarding the omissions, the panel considers that the remarks of the Honourable Justice Nadon in Sanchez8 do apply in this case. He stated: [9] Thus, in my opinion it was completely reasonable for the Refugee Division to take a dim view of the fact that the applicant had omitted several significant facts. In Basseghi v. M.C.I., [1994] F.C.J. No. 1867, Teitelbaum J. stated: It is not incorrect to say that answers given in a PIF should be brief but it is incorrect to say that the answers should not be complete with all of the relevant facts. It is not enough for an applicant to say that what he said in oral testimony was an elaboration. All relevant and important facts should be included in one's PIF. The oral evidence should go on to explain the information contained in the PIP. [Emphasis added]

As for the female claimant, when questioned about the problems she experienced in Croatia, the female claimant stated [translation] "I do not have a lot of experience. I have only eight years of schooling. At school, I was mistreated, spit on, and insulted because I am a gypsy."

When asked to be more specific regarding the threats and attacks she suffered during those last years in Croatia, the female claimant stated spontaneously, [translation] "On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, when I was going out to collect garbage at the dump, there were some Croats downtown; this is where we find plastic bottles. They threw bottles at me. They shouted gypsy at me, spit on me and insulted me. They said bad words to me and said to blow them (sex). They tried to tear my clothes. I managed to get on my bicycle and escape. It is like that back home; they look at nationality."
When questioned about whether she had experienced other similar incidents, the female claimant stated that, each weekend, she was harassed by Croats when she went downtown.

Given that the female claimant responded to the questions in a direct, spontaneous and unexaggerated manner, the panel finds that she is a trustworthy witness, especially as she seemed to have been deeply affected by the events she stated she experienced in Croatia.

Also, to arrive at this conclusion, the panel took into consideration that the intimidation and sexual harassment against the female claimant, taken cumulatively, amounts to persecution. Furthermore, in its analysis, the panel took into account the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.9 CONCLUSION

Having analyzed the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the male claimant, XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection." Therefore, the panel rejects his refugee protection claim.
As for the female claimant, the panel determines that XXXX XXXX is a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection."

Therefore, the panel allows her refugee protection claim. Jean-Guy Jam Me Jean-Guy Jam March 17, 2014 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, (a) is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries; or (b) not having a country of nationality, is outside the country of their former habitual residence and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to return to that country. 2 97. (1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care. 3 Exhibit A-2: Immigration documents. 4 Exhibit P-1: Male claimant's Personal Information Form. 5 Exhibit R-4: Document from the XXXXX hospital. 6 Exhibit R-5: Bill from the XXXXX hospital. 7 Exhibit A-2: Immigration documents, IMM5611. 8 Sanchez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2000 CanLII 15189 (FC). 9 Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.
